Action Plan:
1) Acute reaction after bee/wasp sting with concern about breathing:
   - Remote visual assessment performed (lips/oral cavity/throat; breathing observed). No visible lip/oral swelling; breathing and speech normal.
   - Start an oral antihistamine: chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg, 1 tablet, up to 6 times per day; OTC purchase acceptable. Alternatively, a non-sedating “one-a-day” antihistamine may be used (specific product/dose not documented).
   - Safety-net: If any swelling of lips/tongue, voice change, stridor, wheeze, increasing shortness of breath, dizziness/syncope, generalized hives, or rapid progression of symptoms occur, go to Emergency Department immediately or call emergency services.
   - Monitor sting site. If redness spreads, becomes hot, painful, or systemic signs develop (fever/malaise), seek reassessment to consider antibiotics (penicillin allergy noted).
   - Educational link on anaphylaxis to be provided for symptom awareness.
   - No allergy testing needed now; consider evaluation only if reactions recur or non-specific rashes develop.
   - Follow-up with the clinic if symptoms persist, worsen, or for reassurance if anxiety increases.
2) Anxiety related to the event:
   - Reassurance provided; advised low threshold to recontact if anxiety or symptoms worsen.

Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Reason for visit: Difficulty breathing and anxiety after recent bee/wasp sting; local rash at sting site; subjective mild right-sided lip swelling; tongue “feels weird.”
- Onset/duration: Sting occurred minutes before the consult.
- Course/severity: Patient does not feel acutely breathless now; sought reassurance due to concern symptoms might worsen.
- Past medical history: Eczema; occasional anxiety/panic symptoms. No known history of anaphylaxis. No prior EpiPen.
- Medications: None taken yet for this episode.
- Social: Works as a computer scientist; lives alone; has a cat.
- Allergies: Penicillin.

Objective:
- General/respiratory (video): Breathing appears normal; speaking in full sentences; no audible stridor/wheeze.
- Oropharynx/lips (video): No visible lip swelling; oropharyngeal view unremarkable.
- Skin (right/left arm as shown): Localized slight redness/blotchiness with puncture mark at sting site; patient reports no notable swelling; clinician did not observe marked swelling.
- Vitals: Not provided.
- Investigations: None.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Bee/wasp sting with localized reaction and concern about breathing:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Localized allergic/inflammatory reaction to Hymenoptera sting (High likelihood per DDx).
   - Differential diagnosis:
     • Early anaphylaxis (IgE-mediated) to Hymenoptera sting (Medium): Supporting—immediate onset after sting, subjective dyspnea and oral sensations; Opposing—no visible swelling, normal breathing/speech, no systemic features, no progression during visit.  
     • Anxiety/panic-related dyspnea (Medium): Supporting—history of anxiety, normal observed respiration; Opposing—temporal association with sting and oral sensations.  
     • Histaminergic angioedema limited to lips/tongue (Low): No visible swelling or airway compromise.  
     • Early cellulitis at sting site (Low): Unlikely minutes after sting; area not hot or expanding.
   - Investigations planned: None at this time.
   - Treatment planned:
     • Start chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet up to 6 times daily; OTC.  
     • Alternatively use a non-sedating “one-a-day” antihistamine (specific product/dose not documented).
     • Safety-net for red flags (lip/tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, stridor, wheeze, voice change, generalized hives, syncope, rapid progression): attend Emergency Department urgently.
     • Monitor for local infection; if spreading erythema/heat/tenderness or systemic features occur, seek review to consider antibiotics (avoid penicillins due to allergy).
     • Educational link on anaphylaxis provided.
   - Relevant referrals: None now; Emergency Department if red flags develop.

2. Anxiety related to acute sting:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Anxiety/panic-related dyspnea (Medium likelihood per DDx).
   - Differential diagnosis: As above under Issue 1.
   - Investigations planned: None.
   - Treatment planned: Reassurance; advised to recontact if anxiety persists or worsens, or if new physical symptoms develop.
   - Relevant referrals: None at this time.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: No vitals (HR, RR, BP, SpO2); no full medication reconciliation; tobacco/alcohol history not obtained; immunization history not discussed. “One-a-day” antihistamine product and exact dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Transcript vs DDx conflicts: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor inaudible/elliptical segments but clinical content adequate.
